extracted.intended_audience: ICLR reviewers, area chairs, conference organizers, and researchers building AI-assisted peer-review tools
extracted.subtask_description: Concrete review guidelines and evaluation protocol for ICLR-style conference peer review, including per-dimension criteria (quality, clarity, significance, originality), numerical scoring scales, an overall 1–10 decision scale, confidence ratings, and an LLM-assisted automated 'report card' scoring framework used in experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefly summarize the paper and its contributions. This is not the place to critique the paper; the authors should generally agree with a well-written summary. This is also not the place to paste the abstract — please provide the summary in your own understanding after reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise statement of the paper's contributions in your own words; avoid copying the abstract or using this section for critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengths and Weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a thorough assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of the paper. A good mental framing is to think of reasons you might accept or reject the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Touch on the key dimensions (quality, clarity, significance, originality) and produce reasons for acceptance/rejection that are concrete and actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality (technical soundness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission technically sound? Are claims well supported (e.g., by theoretical analysis or experimental results)? Are the methods appropriate? Is this a complete piece of work or work in progress? Are the authors careful and honest about evaluating both strengths and weaknesses?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess correctness, appropriateness of methods, sufficiency of evidence (theory/experiments), and the thoroughness/honesty of evaluation. Base the numerical 'Quality' rating on this discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission clearly written and well organized? Does it adequately inform the reader?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that a superbly written paper provides enough information for an expert reader to reproduce results. If clarity is lacking, make constructive suggestions for improvement (e.g., reorganize sections, clarify notation, add examples). Base the numerical 'Clarity' rating on this discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results impactful for the community? Are other researchers or practitioners likely to use the ideas or build on them? Does the submission address a difficult task in a better way than previous work? Does it demonstrably advance understanding of the topic?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider breadth and depth of impact, novelty of insights or data, and whether the contribution enables future work. Base the numerical 'Significance' rating on this discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work provide new insights, deepen understanding, or highlight important properties of existing methods? Is it clear how this work differs from previous contributions, with relevant citations provided? Does the work introduce novel tasks or methods?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality may include novel combinations of existing techniques or empirical/theoretical insights; it does not require an entirely new method. Base the numerical 'Originality' rating on this discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-dimension numerical ratings (Quality, Clarity, Significance, Originality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign numerical ratings for Quality, Clarity, Significance, and Originality on a 4-point scale: 4 = excellent, 3 = good, 2 = fair, 1 = poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These ratings should be based on the Strengths and Weaknesses discussion. Use them to communicate relative strengths across the four dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions (actionable suggestions)
rubrics_metrics.description: List and carefully describe questions and suggestions for the authors which should focus on key points, ideally around 3–5, that are actionable with clear guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of items where an author response can change your opinion, clarify confusion, or address a limitation. You are strongly encouraged to state clear criteria under which your evaluation score could increase or decrease; this is important for productive rebuttal and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and Negative Societal Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the authors adequately addressed the limitations and potential negative societal impact of their work? If so, simply leave 'yes'; if not, include constructive suggestions for improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be rewarded rather than punished for being upfront about limitations. Provide concrete recommendations for mitigating risks and discussing broader impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall score (1–10 decision scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an overall score for the submission on a 1–10 scale with explicit choice labels: 10 Strong Accept, 9 Accept, 8 Weak Accept, 7 Borderline Accept, 6 Weak Reject, 5 Reject, 4 Strong Reject, 3 Serious Reject, 2 Severe Reject, 1 Desk Reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the detailed descriptions for each integer to map the paper's combination of technical quality, impact, evaluation quality, reproducibility, and ethical considerations into a single overall decision-oriented score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence score
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a confidence score (1–5) to indicate how confident you are in your evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 = absolutely certain (very familiar and checked details carefully); 4 = confident but not absolute; 3 = fairly confident (possible gaps); 2 = willing to defend but likely gaps; 1 = educated guess (not in-area or difficult to understand). Use this to communicate reliability of your assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: Publicity of reviews and metareviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Reminder that after decisions are made, reviews and metareviews of accepted papers and opted-in rejected papers will be made public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing reviews, be mindful of public visibility; maintain professional tone and avoid making unsubstantiated or defamatory statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated 'Report Card' dimensions (Coverage, Specificity, Evidence Base, Constructiveness & Tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: An LLM-generated multi-dimensional report card rates reviews on: Coverage (touches novelty, significance, technical soundness, presentation), Specificity (actionability, page/line references, concrete rewrites), Evidence Base (quotations, equations, empirical numbers to substantiate claims), and Constructiveness & Tone (politeness, professional encouragement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each dimension is scored 1 (Poor)–5 (Excellent). Weights used in the illustration: Coverage 0.30, Specificity 0.25, Evidence Base 0.20, Constructiveness & Tone 0.25. The system produces a weighted composite (e.g., 3.1 / 5) to summarize overall review quality. Use the report card to surface overlooked dimensions and nudge reviewers toward evidence-based, actionable critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report Card: Strengths Detected & Areas for Improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The automated system should list detected strengths (e.g., concise summary, concrete missing elements, constructive tone) and targeted areas for improvement (e.g., request deeper evidence, broader coverage, finer-grained actionables, minor language edits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete examples (e.g., suggest Fig. 2 showing X or correct typographical slips) to operationalize feedback. Use the card strategically (before author response and again after rebuttal) to improve review depth without extending timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM-as-Judge semantic-coverage protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation protocol for measuring semantic overlap between human reviews and AI-generated points: count distinct points raised in the real statement (make a checklist), then count how many generated points overlap and return the scalar number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Return format: 'Real points: <number> - [<point1>, <point2>, …] Hits (overlap): <number>'. Use an LLM-as-judge to determine whether each human point was semantically captured by the AI; this is used to assess coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation notes: LLM-as-Judge and RAG grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes on evaluation emphasize prompting a powerful LLM (the 'judge') with human review points and AI-generated points to assess semantic coverage. For grounding and fact-checking, use Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judge should determine for each human point if it was semantically captured by the AI. Use retrieval to support factual claims and reduce hallucinations when generating review components.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICL prompt and few-shot input structure for review-component generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt engineering structure: include REVIEW_GUIDELINES, few-shot examples (paper title, abstract, content, human review comments), then request LLM to infer potential strengths, weaknesses, initial score, initial review, and generate author rebuttal if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide multiple exemplars demonstrating desired output formats (POTENTIAL_STRENGTHS, POTENTIAL_WEAKNESSES, INITIAL_SCORE, INITIAL_REVIEW, AUTHOR_REBUTTAL). Include paper title, abstract, and content in inputs when available. This structure guides LLM outputs to be aligned with human review conventions.
